subjective.hpi:
The patient is a 29-year-old female with no significant past medical history, presenting for a routine check-up with a complaint of right knee pain.

Right Knee Pain
The patient reports right knee pain that began three to four days ago after starting cycling exercise classes, which involve spin activities. The pain is localized to the right knee, described as dull and intermittent, and does not occur all day. It is aggravated by standing for long periods, walking uphill, running, and climbing stairs, and is relieved by sitting or resting. She took a painkiller once at the onset, which provided some relief, though she is unsure if improvement was due to rest or medication. She is not regularly using ice or a knee wrap. The patient denies any prior knee injuries or surgeries and has not experienced the knee giving out. She is generally healthy, does not take any regular medications, and has no allergies. Family history is notable for hypertension in her father and low blood pressure in her mother. She has had one prior surgery for a dental cyst, unrelated to her current complaint.

A therapeutic corticosteroid injection was performed to reduce inflammation and facilitate improved function. During today’s wellness visit, the patient initiated and reaffirmed an ongoing, continuous primary care relationship. Management of her musculoskeletal complaint requires longitudinal oversight, including monitoring response to conservative therapy, guidance on graded return to exercise, injury-prevention counseling, and assessment for potential escalation if symptoms do not improve. Her care plan will require personalized follow-up to support her long-term health goals, integrate preventive services, and proactively manage emerging issues. The complexity and continuity of this relationship extend beyond today’s singular knee complaint and involve a holistic, patient-specific approach to ongoing primary care. Wellness exam done ;Right knee sprain
- Assessment consistent with right knee sprain based on localized pain, exam findings, and recent increase in physical activity; no evidence of structural injury requiring imaging.
- Recommend rest and avoidance of spinning or strenuous activity for at least one week.
- Gradual return to exercise, starting with walking.
- Use knee brace when resuming exercise.
- Over-the-counter pain medications (Ibuprofen, Motrin, Advil) as needed.
- Nurse to provide knee exercises.

Chief Complaint
RM 310; Subsequent Medicare Annual Wellness Visit. Has form for [OCCUPATION]. Big toe (right foot) toenail concerns.

History of Present Illness
The patient is a [AGE] male with a history of heart attack and coronary artery disease, presenting for a subsequent Medicare Annual Wellness Visit. Prior initial Medicare Annual Wellness Visit G0438 was completed more than 12 months ago. No AWV or IPPE has been billed in the past 12 months.   Heart Attack and Coronary Artery Disease The patient reports having had a heart attack, which he attributes to stress from being [OCCUPATION] after a layoff last year. He has a family history of heart disease. He is currently attending cardiac rehab and notes that his blood pressure has improved and he feels better physically. He denies any current chest pain or shortness of breath. He is not experiencing any significant issues with his current medications.   Onychomycosis of Great Toe The patient has had a fungal infection in his right great toenail for many years, which has recently worsened. [PARENTHOOD] attempted to treat it, resulting in the nail cracking. The patient reports that the infection is also present in his small toe but to a lesser extent. He is interested in treatment options and is informed about an antifungal pill that takes about three months to show improvement. He is concerned about the impact of the medication on his cardiac health, but it is clarified that the medication is metabolized by the liver and does not affect the heart.   Elevated Liver Enzymes and Hyperlipidemia The patient has a history of elevated liver enzymes, which have been monitored due to his hyperlipidemia. His liver function tests were normal during his last checkup. He has been managing his hyperlipidemia with diet and exercise. He reports that he has made some changes to his diet and exercise routine, although he is not engaging in intense physical activity. He previously experienced backaches, which he suspected were related to his statin medication. After switching to a different statin and lowering the dose, the backaches have resolved.
